#| autorun: true
#| include: false
# Pre-build every name the page uses, so each cell works no matter which
# cells were run before it. The visible cells re-derive all of this.
class Node:
    def __init__(self, name="", length=0.0):
        self.name = name
        self.length = length
        self.children = []
        self.parent = None
    def is_leaf(self):
        return not self.children
    def leaves(self):
        return [self] if self.is_leaf() else [l for c in self.children for l in c.leaves()]
    def walk(self):
        yield self
        for c in self.children:
            yield from c.walk()

def parse_newick(text):
    s = text.strip().rstrip(";")
    pos = 0
    def read_label():
        nonlocal pos
        if pos < len(s) and s[pos] == "'":
            end = s.index("'", pos + 1)
            label, pos_ = s[pos + 1:end], end + 1
        else:
            start = pos
            pos_ = pos
            while pos_ < len(s) and s[pos_] not in ",():;":
                pos_ += 1
            label = s[start:pos_]
        pos = pos_
        return label.strip()
    def read_length():
        nonlocal pos
        if pos < len(s) and s[pos] == ":":
            pos += 1
            start = pos
            while pos < len(s) and s[pos] not in ",();":
                pos += 1
            return float(s[start:pos])
        return 0.0
    def read_node():
        nonlocal pos
        node = Node()
        if s[pos] == "(":
            pos += 1
            while True:
                child = read_node()
                child.parent = node
                node.children.append(child)
                if s[pos] != ",":
                    break
                pos += 1
            pos += 1
        node.name = read_label()
        node.length = read_length()
        return node
    return read_node()

def set_depths(root):
    for node in root.walk():
        node.depth = (node.parent.depth if node.parent else 0.0) + node.length

def layout(root):
    set_depths(root)
    for i, leaf in enumerate(root.leaves()):
        leaf.y = float(i)
    def place(node):
        if not node.is_leaf():
            for c in node.children:
                place(c)
            node.y = sum(c.y for c in node.children) / len(node.children)
    place(root)

def draw_tree(root, ax, colors=None, default="#555555", lw=0.8,
              labels=False, fontsize=6):
    layout(root)
    segs = {}
    def add(col, x0, y0, x1, y1):
        xs, ys = segs.setdefault(col, ([], []))
        xs += [x0, x1, None]; ys += [y0, y1, None]
    for node in root.walk():
        col = (colors or {}).get(id(node), default)
        if node.parent:
            add(col, node.parent.depth, node.y, node.depth, node.y)
        if not node.is_leaf():
            ys = [c.y for c in node.children]
            add(col, node.depth, min(ys), node.depth, max(ys))
    for col, (xs, ys) in segs.items():
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=col, lw=lw, solid_capstyle="round")
    if labels:
        for leaf in root.leaves():
            col = (colors or {}).get(id(leaf), "#222222")
            ax.text(leaf.depth, leaf.y, " " + leaf.name, va="center",
                    fontsize=fontsize, color=col)
    ax.set_yticks([])
    for side in ("left", "top", "right"):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)

def draw_round(root, ax, colors=None, default="#555555", lw=0.7,
               labels=False, fontsize=5, gap_deg=10):
    layout(root)
    tips = root.leaves()
    max_d = max(t.depth for t in tips)
    span = np.deg2rad(360 - gap_deg)
    a0 = np.deg2rad(90 + gap_deg / 2)
    def ang(y):
        return a0 + span * y / max(len(tips) - 1, 1)
    segs = {}
    def add(col, pts):
        xs, ys = segs.setdefault(col, ([], []))
        xs += [p[0] for p in pts] + [None]; ys += [p[1] for p in pts] + [None]
    for node in root.walk():
        col = (colors or {}).get(id(node), default)
        if node.parent:
            add(col, [(ang(node.y), node.parent.depth), (ang(node.y), node.depth)])
        if not node.is_leaf():
            ys = sorted(c.y for c in node.children)
            arc = np.linspace(ang(ys[0]), ang(ys[-1]), 24)
            add(col, list(zip(arc, np.full(24, node.depth))))
    for col, (xs, ys) in segs.items():
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=col, lw=lw, solid_capstyle="round")
    if labels:
        for t in tips:
            a = ang(t.y); deg = np.rad2deg(a) % 360
            flip = 90 < deg < 270
            ax.text(a, max_d * 1.02, t.name,
                    rotation=(deg + 180 if flip else deg), rotation_mode="anchor",
                    ha="right" if flip else "left", va="center", fontsize=fontsize,
                    color=(colors or {}).get(id(t), "#222222"))
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.spines["polar"].set_visible(False)
    ax.grid(False)

def clade(root, names):
    want = set(names)
    best = None
    for node in root.walk():
        have = {l.name for l in node.leaves()}
        if want <= have and (best is None or len(have) < len(best[0])):
            best = (have, node)
    return best[1] if best else None

def paint(groups):
    colors = {}
    for cl, col in groups:
        for node in cl.walk():
            colors[id(node)] = col
    return colors

mini = parse_newick("((Homo:6.7, Pan:6.7):2.2, Gorilla:8.9);")
set_depths(mini)

amniotes = parse_newick(open_url(DATA_URL + "amniotes_family.nwk").read())
set_depths(amniotes)
root_age = max(l.depth for l in amniotes.leaves())
primates = clade(amniotes, ["Hominidae", "Lemuridae"])

amniote_rows = [line.split(",") for line in
                open_url(DATA_URL + "amniote_species.csv").read().strip().split("\n")[1:]]
primate_families = sorted({r[2] for r in amniote_rows if r[1] == "Primates"})

taxonomy = Node("Amniota")
index = {}
for r in amniote_rows:
    parent = taxonomy
    for name in (r[0], r[1], r[2]):
        key = (parent.name, name)
        child = index.get(key)
        if child is None:
            child = Node(name, length=1.0)
            child.parent = parent
            parent.children.append(child)
            index[key] = child
        parent = child
fams = taxonomy.leaves()

euk = parse_newick(open_url(DATA_URL + "eukaryotes_class.nwk").read())
set_depths(euk)
euk_age = max(l.depth for l in euk.leaves())
side_a, side_b = euk.children
block_1, block_2 = side_a.children
fungi = block_1
small_1, rest = block_2.children
animals, small_2 = rest.children
plants = clade(euk, ["Magnoliopsida", "Chlorophyceae"])
block = plants
colors = paint([(animals, "#4269d0"), (fungi, "#e66852"), (plants, "#30a8b1")])

phyla = parse_newick(open_url(DATA_URL + "eukaryotes_phylum.nwk").read())
set_depths(phyla)
phyla_age = max(l.depth for l in phyla.leaves())

## 1 · A "tree" from Part A

In Part A you worked with a **table** of amniotes: one row per species.
This data is **hierarchical**: each species
belongs to exactly one group, each group to exactly one larger group, and
so on up to a single root. The
taxonomy columns of Part A's amniote table, where every species sits in a
genus, every genus in a family, every family in an order, and every order
in a class. This is the structure a **tree** draws: one
parent per item, one root, with no cycles.

Part A's table
contains a tree which can be built with a node structure layout that gives every node
two coordinates (x is distance from the root; y spreads the tips one per
row, with each ancestor centred on its children).



```{pyodide}
class Node:
    def __init__(self, name="", length=0.0):
        self.name = name          # taxon name (tips) or support label (internal)
        self.length = length      # branch length to the parent, in Myr here
        self.children = []        # empty list = this node is a tip
        self.parent = None

    def is_leaf(self):
        return not self.children

    def leaves(self):
        return [self] if self.is_leaf() else [l for c in self.children for l in c.leaves()]

    def walk(self):
        yield self
        for c in self.children:
            yield from c.walk()


def set_depths(root):
    for node in root.walk():
        node.depth = (node.parent.depth if node.parent else 0.0) + node.length


def layout(root):
    set_depths(root)
    for i, leaf in enumerate(root.leaves()):
        leaf.y = float(i)
    def place(node):
        if not node.is_leaf():
            for c in node.children:
                place(c)
            node.y = sum(c.y for c in node.children) / len(node.children)
    place(root)


def draw_tree(root, ax, colors=None, default="#555555", lw=0.8,
              labels=False, fontsize=6):
    layout(root)
    segs = {}                     # colour -> one long broken line
    def add(col, x0, y0, x1, y1):
        xs, ys = segs.setdefault(col, ([], []))
        xs += [x0, x1, None]; ys += [y0, y1, None]
    for node in root.walk():
        col = (colors or {}).get(id(node), default)
        if node.parent:                                   # horizontal branch
            add(col, node.parent.depth, node.y, node.depth, node.y)
        if not node.is_leaf():                            # vertical connector
            ys = [c.y for c in node.children]
            add(col, node.depth, min(ys), node.depth, max(ys))
    for col, (xs, ys) in segs.items():
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=col, lw=lw, solid_capstyle="round")
    if labels:
        for leaf in root.leaves():
            col = (colors or {}).get(id(leaf), "#222222")
            ax.text(leaf.depth, leaf.y, " " + leaf.name, va="center",
                    fontsize=fontsize, color=col)
    ax.set_yticks([])
    for side in ("left", "top", "right"):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
```

Now the tree itself. Walk the table's rows and create a node the first
time each class, order and family name appears:

```{pyodide}
text = open_url(DATA_URL + "amniote_species.csv").read()
rows = [line.split(",") for line in text.strip().split("\n")[1:]]

taxonomy = Node("Amniota")
index = {}
for r in rows:
    parent = taxonomy
    for name in (r[0], r[1], r[2]):          # class > order > family
        key = (parent.name, name)
        child = index.get(key)
        if child is None:
            child = Node(name, length=1.0)
            child.parent = parent
            parent.children.append(child)
            index[key] = child
        parent = child

fams = taxonomy.leaves()
print(f"{len(fams)} families, {len(index) - len(fams)} classes and orders above them")
```

```{pyodide}
assert len(fams) == 465
assert len(taxonomy.children) == 3
assert sum(len(c.children) for c in taxonomy.children) == 72
print("✓ 465 families in 72 orders in 3 classes, exactly as the columns nest")
```

This first tree is a hierarchy, not a dated phylogeny. Put each taxonomic rank
in its own categorical column and draw every node explicitly. The horizontal
spacing separates ranks; it does not measure evolutionary distance or time.

```{pyodide}
layout(taxonomy)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 8))

# Give each class one colour, then carry that colour down all its branches.
class_colours = {
    "Mammalia": "#2764C7",
    "Aves": "#D86B18",
    "Reptilia": "#12806A",
}
class_labels = {
    "Mammalia": "Mammalia (mammals)",
    "Aves": "Aves (birds)",
    "Reptilia": "Reptilia (reptiles)",
}

def class_of(node):
    """Return the class immediately below the Amniota root."""
    branch = node
    while branch.parent is not None and branch.parent is not taxonomy:
        branch = branch.parent
    return None if branch is taxonomy else branch.name

# Group parent-child lines by class so all descendant branches inherit colour.
edges = {name: ([], []) for name in class_colours}
for node in taxonomy.walk():
    if node.parent is not None:
        edge_x, edge_y = edges[class_of(node)]
        edge_x.extend([node.parent.depth, node.depth, None])
        edge_y.extend([node.parent.y, node.y, None])

for class_name, (edge_x, edge_y) in edges.items():
    ax.plot(edge_x, edge_y, color=class_colours[class_name],
            lw=0.55, alpha=0.75, zorder=1)

# A point is a node. Plot each rank separately so the hierarchy is visible.
rank_sizes = {0: 85, 1: 42, 2: 15, 3: 7}
for rank, size in rank_sizes.items():
    nodes = [node for node in taxonomy.walk() if node.depth == rank]
    colours = [
        "#1f3b5d" if node is taxonomy else class_colours[class_of(node)]
        for node in nodes
    ]
    ax.scatter(
        [node.depth for node in nodes],
        [node.y for node in nodes],
        s=size,
        color=colours,
        edgecolors="white" if rank < 2 else "none",
        linewidths=0.6,
        zorder=3,
    )

# Label the single root and the three class nodes.
ax.annotate("Amniota", (taxonomy.depth, taxonomy.y),
            xytext=(-8, 0), textcoords="offset points",
            ha="right", va="center", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold")
for class_node in taxonomy.children:
    ax.annotate(class_labels[class_node.name],
                (class_node.depth, class_node.y),
                xytext=(9, -11), textcoords="offset points",
                ha="left", va="top", fontsize=8,
                color=class_colours[class_node.name], fontweight="bold",
                zorder=5,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.22", facecolor="white",
                          edgecolor="none", alpha=0.94))

ax.set_xticks([0, 1, 2, 3])
ax.set_xticklabels(["ROOT\n1 node", "CLASS\n3 nodes",
                    "ORDER\n72 nodes", "FAMILY\n465 nodes"])
ax.xaxis.tick_top()
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=0, pad=9)
ax.set_xlim(-0.28, 3.08)
ax.set_ylim(-8, len(fams) + 7)
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.grid(axis="x", color="#e8ebef", linewidth=0.8, zorder=0)
for side in ("left", "right", "top", "bottom"):
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
ax.set_title("Three Classes of Amniote Families", pad=42)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Each dot is now countable: one root, three classes, 72 orders and 465
families. A line means "belongs to". Colour traces each of the three classes
from its class node through all of its orders and families. The vertical
ordering only keeps each parent near its children; it does not make
neighbouring orders more closely related. The table records membership at
four ranks, not evolutionary distances between the groups.


## 2 · Phylogenetic trees

The word *phylogenetic* comes from *phylogeny*: Greek *phylon* (a tribe,
kind or lineage) and *-geneia* (origin). Ernst Haeckel coined the German word
*Phylogenie* in 1866 for the evolutionary history of a group. A phylogenetic
tree is therefore a diagram of a hypothesis about descent and shared origins.

A phylogenetic tree has three kinds of parts:

- **Tips** (leaves) are observed things: living species, families,
  classes.
- **Internal nodes** are inferred ancestors: "these two lineages were once
  one population." Each is a hypothesis.
- **Branch lengths**, in the trees on this page, are **time**: a branch of
  length 6.7 means 6.7 million years of independent evolution.

Haeckel introduces the tree metaphor in this 1866 genealogy of mammals:
ancestry grows from a trunk and living groups occupy the outer branches. The
form makes hierarchy immediately legible, but its branch lengths are not a
measured time scale. Modern phylogenetic trees retain the branching structure
while treating topology and branch length as claims supported by data.

![Ernst Haeckel's 1866 *Stammbaum der Säugethiere mit Inbegriff des Menschen*
(family tree of mammals, including humans). [Source image: Johns Hopkins
University Press.](https://jhupress.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/08/pg-110.jpg)](../images/haeckel-mammal-tree-1866.jpg){#fig-haeckel-mammals width=52% fig-alt="A black-and-white nineteenth-century genealogy of mammals drawn as a large branching tree, with Mammalia at the trunk and named mammal groups on the branches."}

Branch length is estimated from genetics.
DNA sequences for the same gene can be compared across many species.
Mutations accumulate at a roughly steady rate, so differences in the sequences is proportional to the time
since lineages separated, giving the *relative* ages.
To turn relative ages into *absolute* ages (millions of years ago), the tree is calibrated
against fossils whose age and position are known.




[TimeTree](https://timetree.org) (Kumar et al. 2022) provides data sets on relationships between species
that invludes evolutionary dates, suitable for constructing a proper phylogenetic tree. TimeTree aggregates thousands of such published studies into consensus
dated trees.


| File | Tips | What one tip is |
|---|---|---|
| `amniotes_family.nwk` | 956 | one family of amniotes (mammals, birds, reptiles) |
| `eukaryotes_class.nwk` | 235 | one class of eukaryotes: animals, fungi, plants, protists |
| `eukaryotes_phylum.nwk` | 66 | one phylum of eukaryotes |


Before we can draw a tree we need it as data. The standard format,
**Newick**, writes a tree as nested parentheses: each pair of parentheses
is one internal node (one ancestor), and `:number` after a name is the
branch length.

Here is one you can read by eye: humans, chimps and
gorillas, with TimeTree's ages in millions of years (Myr):

```
((Homo:6.7, Pan:6.7):2.2, Gorilla:8.9);
```

Read from the inside out: `Homo` and `Pan` each sit at the end of a
6.7-Myr branch from their shared ancestor, so the human–chimp split was
6.7 million years ago. That ancestor connects, 2.2 Myr further back, to
the ancestor it shares with `Gorilla`: 6.7 + 2.2 = 8.9 Myr, exactly
`Gorilla`'s own branch length.

In a dated tree every tip is the same total
distance from the root, because every living lineage has had the same
amount of time.

The format is recursive (a tree is a node whose children are trees), so
the parser is recursive too, reusing the `Node` class from Section 1.


```{pyodide}
def parse_newick(text):
    s = text.strip().rstrip(";")
    pos = 0

    def read_label():
        nonlocal pos
        if pos < len(s) and s[pos] == "'":            # quoted label, e.g. '90'
            end = s.index("'", pos + 1)
            label, pos = s[pos + 1:end], end + 1
        else:
            start = pos
            while pos < len(s) and s[pos] not in ",():;":
                pos += 1
            label = s[start:pos]
        return label.strip()

    def read_length():
        nonlocal pos
        if pos < len(s) and s[pos] == ":":            # ":6.7" = branch length
            pos += 1
            start = pos
            while pos < len(s) and s[pos] not in ",();":
                pos += 1
            return float(s[start:pos])
        return 0.0

    def read_node():
        nonlocal pos
        node = Node()
        if s[pos] == "(":                             # "(" = ancestor: recurse
            pos += 1
            while True:
                child = read_node()
                child.parent = node
                node.children.append(child)
                if s[pos] != ",":
                    break
                pos += 1
            pos += 1                                  # consume ")"
        node.name = read_label()
        node.length = read_length()
        return node

    return read_node()


mini = parse_newick("((Homo:6.7, Pan:6.7):2.2, Gorilla:8.9);")
print("tips:", [l.name for l in mini.leaves()])
```

```{pyodide}
assert [l.name for l in mini.leaves()] == ["Homo", "Pan", "Gorilla"]
assert mini.children[0].children[0].name == "Homo"
assert mini.children[0].children[0].length == 6.7
print("✓ parser reads tips, structure and branch lengths correctly")
```

## 3 · Drawing dated trees

The taxonomy tree's x axis was rank. In a dated tree the branch lengths
are millions of years, so the same `draw_tree` now puts **time** on the x
axis.

Draw the hominid mini-tree first:

```{pyodide}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.6))
draw_tree(mini, ax, labels=True, fontsize=11)
ax.margins(y=0.18)
ax.set_xlabel("Myr since the root")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Now a tree with every family of **amniotes**, the same group
whose species table you cleaned in Part A.

```{pyodide}
amniotes = parse_newick(open_url(DATA_URL + "amniotes_family.nwk").read())
set_depths(amniotes)
root_age = max(l.depth for l in amniotes.leaves())
print(f"{len(amniotes.leaves())} families, root {root_age:.1f} Myr ago")
```

The mini-tree used **Myr since the root**, which matches the stored branch
depths but is not the most natural way to read historical dates. For this
larger tree, label the axis in **millions of years ago**: about 319 at the root,
counting down to 0 at the living tips. Only the tick labels are reversed; the
tree geometry and branch lengths do not change.

```{pyodide}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 7))
draw_tree(amniotes, ax, lw=0.4)

mya_labels = [round(root_age), 250, 200, 150, 100, 50, 0]
depth_ticks = [0] + [root_age - age for age in mya_labels[1:]]
ax.set_xticks(depth_ticks)
ax.set_xticklabels(mya_labels)
ax.set_xlim(0, root_age * 1.02)
ax.set_xlabel("millions of years ago")
ax.set_title(f"{len(amniotes.leaves())} Amniote Families")
plt.show()
```

No labels (at 956 tips they would be too many).

The shape shows how every mammal, bird and reptile family trace back to **one node** ~319 Myr
ago. The big early fork near the root is mammals splitting
from the reptile-plus-bird lineage. Reading left to right now also reads as
deep past to present: the numbers decrease from about 319 million years ago to
0, rather than increasing as distance from the root.

::: {.callout-note title="A class is not necessarily a clade"}
Part A records `Aves` (birds) and `Reptilia` as separate classes. On the
phylogenetic tree, however, birds descend from within the reptile lineage:
birds are living dinosaurs and therefore part of the reptile **clade**.
"Reptiles" with birds removed is not a complete clade because it leaves out
some descendants of their common ancestor.
:::

## 4 · Clades and common ancestors

A **clade** is an ancestor plus *all* of its descendants: a complete
subtree, snapped off at one internal node. "Mammals" is a clade;
"cold-blooded animals" is not, because their common ancestor also has
warm-blooded descendants. Clades are groups that a tree can
point at through the **MRCA**, the most
recent common ancestor for a group of tips.

```{pyodide}
def clade(root, names):
    """Smallest clade whose tips include every name in `names` (their MRCA)."""
    want = set(names)
    best = None
    for node in root.walk():
        have = {l.name for l in node.leaves()}
        if want <= have and (best is None or len(have) < len(best[0])):
            best = (have, node)
    return best[1] if best else None


primates = clade(amniotes, ["Hominidae", "Lemuridae"])
print(f"{len(primates.leaves())} families, crown age "
      f"{root_age - primates.depth:.1f} Myr")
```

The `clade` function returns the
*smallest* branch containing both descendants. Hominidae and Lemuridae sit on
opposite sides of the deepest split within Primates, so naming them
recovers all 19 primate families, every one descended from the same ancestor
~74 Myr ago. Two families from the same side would return a smaller
branch: Hominidae and Hylobatidae would give just the apes.

```{pyodide}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.8, 4.6))
draw_tree(primates, ax, labels=True, fontsize=9, default="#4269d0")
ax.margins(x=0.16)
for label in ax.texts:
    if label.get_text().strip() == "Hominidae":
        label.set_fontweight("bold")
ticks = range(0, 80, 10)
ax.set_xticks([root_age - t for t in ticks])
ax.set_xticklabels([str(t) for t in ticks])
ax.set_xlabel("Myr ago")
ax.set_title("The 19 Primate Families")
plt.show()
```

`Hominidae` (all great apes,
including humans) is one twig among nineteen. 
`Paleopropithecidae`, the
sloth lemurs, are **extinct**: humans reached Madagascar roughly two
thousand years ago, and the last sloth lemurs disappeared around 500
years ago. A dated tree can carry recently-lost lineages alongside
living ones, with nothing in the drawing itself marking them as extinct.

### Taxonomy columns versus a phylogeny

Section 1 built the tree encoded by Part A's hierarchical columns. Now that we can obtain
a dated clade, compare the two side-by-side:

```{pyodide}
text = open_url(DATA_URL + "amniote_species.csv").read()
rows = [line.split(",") for line in text.strip().split("\n")[1:]]
primate_families = sorted({r[2] for r in rows if r[1] == "Primates"})

star = Node("Primates")
for name in primate_families:
    tip = Node(name, length=1.0)
    tip.parent = star
    star.children.append(tip)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 5.5))
draw_tree(star, axes[0], labels=True, fontsize=9)
axes[0].set_title(f"Part A's taxonomy: {len(primate_families)} families, one node")
axes[0].set_xticks([])
draw_tree(primates, axes[1], labels=True, fontsize=9, default="#4269d0")
axes[1].set_title("TimeTree: the same clade, resolved and dated")
ticks = range(0, 80, 20)
axes[1].set_xticks([root_age - t for t in ticks])
axes[1].set_xticklabels([str(t) for t in ticks])
axes[1].set_xlabel("Myr ago")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The right tree makes claims that the left tree cannot make. For example, the claim that apes split from monkeys before
either split from lemurs. Every split has a date.

Compare the family names used by the two sources:

```{pyodide}
import re

table_families = set(primate_families)
tree_tips = [leaf.name for leaf in primates.leaves()]
tree_families = {re.sub(r"-\d+$", "", name) for name in tree_tips}

print(f"life-history table: {len(table_families)} family names")
print(f"TimeTree: {len(tree_tips)} tips, representing "
      f"{len(tree_families)} family names")
print("only in life-history table:",
      sorted(table_families - tree_families))
print("only in TimeTree:",
      sorted(tree_families - table_families))
```

The life-history table uses `Indridae`; TimeTree uses `Indriidae`. They refer
to the same living family. TimeTree also contains `Paleopropithecidae`, the
extinct sloth lemurs, which are absent from the table of living species.

TimeTree has 19 tips because `Cebidae`, `Indriidae` and `Lepilemuridae` each
appear twice, with `-1` and `-2` suffixes. Removing those suffixes leaves 16
family names: the same 15 living families after correcting the spelling, plus
`Paleopropithecidae`.


### Seven living amniote lineages

The Rowe (2017) figure in Part A shows seven living amniote lineages:
Monotremata, Marsupialia, Placentalia, Testudines, Lepidosauria,
Crocodilia and Aves. We will colour the same seven groups on the
956-family tree loaded in Section 3.

For groups recorded in the Part A table, collect their family names and
pass them to `clade()`. The function returns the smallest clade containing
those families. The table does not record Marsupialia or Placentalia as
separate categories. In the tree, Mammalia splits into Monotremata and
Theria, and Theria then splits into Marsupialia and Placentalia. Hominidae
identifies the placental branch; the other branch is Marsupialia.

```{pyodide}
text = open_url(DATA_URL + "amniote_species.csv").read()
rows = [line.split(",") for line in text.strip().split("\n")[1:]]
tip_names = {l.name for l in amniotes.leaves()}

def group_clade(level, name):
    """MRCA of every tree tip that Part A's table puts in the group."""
    col = {"class": 0, "order": 1}[level]
    fams = {r[2] for r in rows if r[col] == name}
    return clade(amniotes, fams & tip_names)

aves  = group_clade("class", "Aves")
tests = group_clade("order", "Testudines")
crocs = group_clade("order", "Crocodilia")
lepid = group_clade("order", "Squamata")     # includes Sphenodontidae, the tuatara
mono  = group_clade("order", "Monotremata")

mam    = group_clade("class", "Mammalia")
theria = next(c for c in mam.children if mono not in list(c.walk()))
a, b   = theria.children                     # Marsupialia and Placentalia
plac   = a if "Hominidae" in {l.name for l in a.leaves()} else b
mars   = b if plac is a else a

lineages = [                                 # listed bottom to top on the tree
    (mars,  "Marsupialia",  "#b5443c"),
    (plac,  "Placentalia",  "#9475cd"),
    (mono,  "Monotremata",  "#c98a00"),
    (lepid, "Lepidosauria", "#30a8b1"),
    (crocs, "Crocodilia",   "#e66852"),
    (aves,  "Aves",         "#4269d0"),
    (tests, "Testudines",   "#d96895"),
]

lineage_colours = {}
for cl, name, col in lineages:
    for node in cl.walk():
        lineage_colours[id(node)] = col

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 7))
draw_tree(amniotes, ax, colors=lineage_colours, lw=0.4)

mya_labels = [round(root_age), 250, 200, 150, 100, 50, 0]
ax.set_xticks([0] + [root_age - age for age in mya_labels[1:]])
ax.set_xticklabels(mya_labels)
ax.set_xlim(0, root_age * 1.02)
ax.set_xlabel("millions of years ago")
ax.legend(handles=[plt.Line2D([], [], color=col, lw=2.5, label=name)
                   for _, name, col in reversed(lineages)],
          loc="upper left", frameon=False, fontsize=9)
ax.set_title("The seven living amniote lineages")
plt.show()
```

The seven clades tile the tree. Notice what is missing: there are no extinct amniote lineages here. TimeTree is
built from DNA comparisons, so every branch must end in an organism
somebody could sequence; a lineage with no living descendants leaves no
tip to sample and vanishes from the tree entirely. The sloth lemurs got
into the primate tree only because they died out ~500 years ago and
left bones young enough for ancient-DNA work. 

### Your turn: Cats and Dogs {#sec-ex-carnivora}

Cats and dogs are both carnivorans. Extract the clade containing
**Canidae** (dogs) and **Felidae** (cats), draw it with labels, and print
how many families it holds and how long ago their common ancestor lived.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_carnivora
import js
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pyodide.http import open_url

DATA_URL = js.location.href.split("site_libs/")[0] + "data/"

class Node:
    def __init__(self, name="", length=0.0):
        self.name = name
        self.length = length
        self.children = []
        self.parent = None
    def is_leaf(self):
        return not self.children
    def leaves(self):
        return [self] if self.is_leaf() else [l for c in self.children for l in c.leaves()]
    def walk(self):
        yield self
        for c in self.children:
            yield from c.walk()

def parse_newick(text):
    s = text.strip().rstrip(";")
    pos = 0
    def read_label():
        nonlocal pos
        if pos < len(s) and s[pos] == "'":
            end = s.index("'", pos + 1)
            label, pos = s[pos + 1:end], end + 1
        else:
            start = pos
            while pos < len(s) and s[pos] not in ",():;":
                pos += 1
            label = s[start:pos]
        return label.strip()
    def read_length():
        nonlocal pos
        if pos < len(s) and s[pos] == ":":
            pos += 1
            start = pos
            while pos < len(s) and s[pos] not in ",();":
                pos += 1
            return float(s[start:pos])
        return 0.0
    def read_node():
        nonlocal pos
        node = Node()
        if s[pos] == "(":
            pos += 1
            while True:
                child = read_node()
                child.parent = node
                node.children.append(child)
                if s[pos] != ",":
                    break
                pos += 1
            pos += 1
        node.name = read_label()
        node.length = read_length()
        return node
    return read_node()

def set_depths(root):
    for node in root.walk():
        node.depth = (node.parent.depth if node.parent else 0.0) + node.length

def layout(root):
    set_depths(root)
    for i, leaf in enumerate(root.leaves()):
        leaf.y = float(i)
    def place(node):
        if not node.is_leaf():
            for c in node.children:
                place(c)
            node.y = sum(c.y for c in node.children) / len(node.children)
    place(root)

def draw_tree(root, ax, colors=None, default="#555555", lw=0.8,
              labels=False, fontsize=6):
    layout(root)
    segs = {}
    def add(col, x0, y0, x1, y1):
        xs, ys = segs.setdefault(col, ([], []))
        xs += [x0, x1, None]; ys += [y0, y1, None]
    for node in root.walk():
        col = (colors or {}).get(id(node), default)
        if node.parent:
            add(col, node.parent.depth, node.y, node.depth, node.y)
        if not node.is_leaf():
            ys = [c.y for c in node.children]
            add(col, node.depth, min(ys), node.depth, max(ys))
    for col, (xs, ys) in segs.items():
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=col, lw=lw, solid_capstyle="round")
    if labels:
        for leaf in root.leaves():
            col = (colors or {}).get(id(leaf), "#222222")
            ax.text(leaf.depth, leaf.y, " " + leaf.name, va="center",
                    fontsize=fontsize, color=col)
    ax.set_yticks([])
    for side in ("left", "top", "right"):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)

def clade(root, names):
    want = set(names)
    best = None
    for node in root.walk():
        have = {l.name for l in node.leaves()}
        if want <= have and (best is None or len(have) < len(best[0])):
            best = (have, node)
    return best[1] if best else None

plt.rcParams.update({
    "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.22, "font.size": 11,
})
amniotes = parse_newick(open_url(DATA_URL + "amniotes_family.nwk").read())
set_depths(amniotes)
root_age = max(l.depth for l in amniotes.leaves())
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_carnivora
# `amniotes` is loaded (956 families) and `root_age` is ~319.
# parse_newick, clade and draw_tree are all defined.

carnivora = ______

print(f"{len(carnivora.leaves())} families, common ancestor "
      f"{root_age - carnivora.depth:.1f} Myr ago")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
______
ax.set_xlabel("Myr since the amniote root")
plt.show()
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_carnivora"}
**Hint 1**: This is the primate example with two different anchor names:
`clade(amniotes, ["Canidae", "Felidae"])`.
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_carnivora"}
**Hint 2**: Draw with
`draw_tree(carnivora, ax, labels=True, fontsize=9)`. You should see 16
families and an ancestor ~55 Myr back.

::: {.solution exercise="ex_carnivora"}
**Fully worked solution:**

```python
carnivora = clade(amniotes, ["Canidae", "Felidae"])

print(f"{len(carnivora.leaves())} families, common ancestor "
      f"{root_age - carnivora.depth:.1f} Myr ago")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
draw_tree(carnivora, ax, labels=True, fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("Myr since the amniote root")
plt.show()
```

16 families from one ancestor ~55 Myr ago. Cats' closest relatives here are the
civets, hyaenas and mongooses. Dogs sit on the other side of the very
first split, nearer to bears and seals. "Cats and dogs" feel like a
natural pair to us, but the clade says they have been separate lineages
almost since the time of dinosaurs.
:::

## 5 · A round tree of life

Rectangular layout runs out of room fast, as tips need vertical space.
A classic fix is to
bend the y-axis into a **circle**, with angle as tip position, and radius
as time.

```{pyodide}
def draw_round(root, ax, colors=None, default="#555555", lw=0.7,
               labels=False, fontsize=5, gap_deg=10):
    layout(root)
    tips = root.leaves()
    max_d = max(t.depth for t in tips)
    span = np.deg2rad(360 - gap_deg)
    a0 = np.deg2rad(90 + gap_deg / 2)         # leave the gap at the top
    def ang(y):
        return a0 + span * y / max(len(tips) - 1, 1)
    segs = {}
    def add(col, pts):
        xs, ys = segs.setdefault(col, ([], []))
        xs += [p[0] for p in pts] + [None]; ys += [p[1] for p in pts] + [None]
    for node in root.walk():
        col = (colors or {}).get(id(node), default)
        if node.parent:                                   # radial branch
            add(col, [(ang(node.y), node.parent.depth), (ang(node.y), node.depth)])
        if not node.is_leaf():                            # connecting arc
            ys = sorted(c.y for c in node.children)
            arc = np.linspace(ang(ys[0]), ang(ys[-1]), 24)
            add(col, list(zip(arc, np.full(24, node.depth))))
    for col, (xs, ys) in segs.items():
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=col, lw=lw, solid_capstyle="round")
    if labels:
        for t in tips:
            a = ang(t.y); deg = np.rad2deg(a) % 360
            flip = 90 < deg < 270                 # keep left-side labels readable
            ax.text(a, max_d * 1.02, t.name,
                    rotation=(deg + 180 if flip else deg), rotation_mode="anchor",
                    ha="right" if flip else "left", va="center", fontsize=fontsize,
                    color=(colors or {}).get(id(t), "#222222"))
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.spines["polar"].set_visible(False)
    ax.grid(False)


def paint(groups):
    """groups: list of (clade_root, colour). Returns {id(node): colour}."""
    colors = {}
    for cl, col in groups:
        for node in cl.walk():
            colors[id(node)] = col
    return colors


euk = parse_newick(open_url(DATA_URL + "eukaryotes_class.nwk").read())
set_depths(euk)
euk_age = max(l.depth for l in euk.leaves())
print(f"{len(euk.leaves())} classes of eukaryotes, root {euk_age:.0f} Myr ago")
```

Draw the whole tree first, with no colouring:

```{pyodide}
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9.5, 9.5))
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="polar")
draw_round(euk, ax, labels=True, fontsize=4.5)
plt.show()
```

Most of the 235 class names around the rim are unfamiliar, but some are
not. `Mammalia`, `Aves` and `Insecta` sit near the sponge classes.
`Magnoliopsida` (the flowering plants) and `Chlorophyceae` (the green
algae) are in a different part of the circle. `Agaricomycetes` (the
mushrooms) is somewhere else again.

### Finding animals, fungi and plants

The three kingdoms are clades somewhere on this tree, but nothing in the
file marks where. We can find them by starting at the root and taking
one split at a time. `paint()` colours a node and everything below it,
so each split can be shown as two colours:

```{pyodide}
side_a, side_b = euk.children
print(len(side_a.leaves()), "classes |", len(side_b.leaves()), "classes")

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9.5, 9.5))
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="polar")
draw_round(euk, ax, colors=paint([(side_a, "#c98a00"), (side_b, "#9475cd")]),
           labels=True, fontsize=4.5)
plt.show()
```

Read the labels. The ochre side has `Mammalia`, `Aves`, `Insecta` and
the sponges, and it also has `Agaricomycetes` and `Saccharomycetes`, the
mushrooms and the yeasts. The purple side has the flowering plants, the
conifers, the green algae and the diatoms. So the first split in the
tree already says something that was not known before DNA sequencing:
fungi sit on the animal side, not the plant side.

Split the ochre side once more:

```{pyodide}
block_1, block_2 = side_a.children
print(len(block_1.leaves()), "and", len(block_2.leaves()), "classes")
print("block 1 examples:", sorted(l.name for l in block_1.leaves())[:4])
```

Every one of the 46 names in the first block ends in `-mycetes`. That
block is the fungi. The other 83 classes are the animals plus a few
single-celled classes, which the next two splits separate out:

```{pyodide}
fungi = block_1

small_1, rest = block_2.children
animals, small_2 = rest.children
print("split off:", [l.name for l in small_1.leaves()],
      "then", [l.name for l in small_2.leaves()])
print(len(animals.leaves()), "classes remain: the animals, sponges to mammals")
```

`Choanoflagellata`, the last class to separate before the animals, are
single-celled filter feeders. They are the closest living relatives of
all animals.

To isolate the plant kingdom on the other side, we need to define what
living things are counted as plants. For this purpose, we will consider
the separation of red algae from green algae to represent the deepest
root of the plant kingdom. A number of other groups (neither plant,
animal, nor fungi) are dropped before reaching that split. Follow the
child that contains `Magnoliopsida` and watch the counts:

```{pyodide}
def side_with(node, name):
    for c in node.children:
        if name in {l.name for l in c.leaves()}:
            return c

block = side_b
for step in range(6):
    block = side_with(block, "Magnoliopsida")
    print("step", step + 1, "->", len(block.leaves()), "classes")
plants = block
```

Steps one to four drop the amoebae, the euglenids, a 51-class block
that holds the diatoms and the ciliates, and the glaucophytes. Step
five is the split we chose as the root: the eight red algae classes
separate from the green line. Step six drops one last single-celled
group, the cryptophytes, which this tree places just inside the green
side of that split. The 32 classes that remain run from green algae to
flowering plants.

Now colour the three kingdoms on one figure.

The colouring works in two steps. `paint()` takes a list of
(clade, colour) pairs. It walks each clade from its top node down
through every descendant and records the colour in a dictionary keyed by
the node's `id()`. `draw_round()` then draws every branch of the tree
and looks each node up in that dictionary. The node's colour is used for
its radial line and for the arc that joins its children. Any node not in
the dictionary gets the `default` colour, grey here, which is how
everything outside the three kingdoms stays grey.

The legend is built by hand. The tree is drawn as bare line segments,
not labelled data series, so matplotlib has nothing to put in a legend
on its own. Each `Line2D` is a stand-in: a short coloured line that
exists only to appear in the legend next to its label.

```{pyodide}
colors = paint([(animals, "#4269d0"), (fungi, "#e66852"), (plants, "#30a8b1")])

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(10.5, 10.5))
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="polar")
draw_round(euk, ax, colors=colors, default="#9a9a9a", labels=True, fontsize=4.5)

from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
ax.legend(handles=[
    Line2D([], [], color="#4269d0", lw=2.5, label=f"Animals ({len(animals.leaves())})"),
    Line2D([], [], color="#e66852", lw=2.5, label=f"Fungi ({len(fungi.leaves())})"),
    Line2D([], [], color="#30a8b1", lw=2.5, label=f"Green plants ({len(plants.leaves())})"),
    Line2D([], [], color="#9a9a9a", lw=2.5, label="Other eukaryotes"),
], loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(-0.05, 1.05), frameon=False, fontsize=9)
plt.show()
```

All animals (sponges to humans) are one blue sector. All of `Mammalia` is a single tick mark.

## 6 · The timetree of life

The round tree is for shape; a **timetree** puts the ages back on a
readable axis. We use the phylum-level file (66 tips) and relabel the
x-axis to run backwards from today, with a few reference events (the Cambrian explosion, the end-Permian extinction event and the end-Cretaceous extinction event that killed the dinosaurs):

```{pyodide}
phyla = parse_newick(open_url(DATA_URL + "eukaryotes_phylum.nwk").read())
set_depths(phyla)
phyla_age = max(l.depth for l in phyla.leaves())
n = len(phyla.leaves())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 10))
draw_tree(phyla, ax, labels=True, fontsize=7)
mya = np.array([1500, 1250, 1000, 750, 500, 250, 0])
ax.set_xticks(phyla_age - mya)
ax.set_xticklabels(mya)
ax.set_xlabel("millions of years ago")
for edge, lab in [(539, "Cambrian begins"), (252, "end-Permian extinction"),
                  (66, "end-Cretaceous extinction")]:
    ax.axvline(phyla_age - edge, color="#bbbbbb", lw=0.7, zorder=0)
    ax.text(phyla_age - edge, n - 0.5, " " + lab, fontsize=7, color="#777777",
            rotation=90, ha="right", va="top")
ax.set_xlim(0, phyla_age * 1.30)
plt.show()
```

Almost every animal phylum was already a separate lineage before the
Cambrian began (the famous "Cambrian explosion" shows up here as a dense burst
of splits just *before* the boundary). No branch ends at either extinction
line: at phylum level, every lineage on this chart survived both of the
worst catastrophes in the fossil record.

Because branch lengths are time, "when did X and Y split?" is the root's age minus the depth of the two tips' MRCA:

```{pyodide}
print(f"chordates vs arthropods (us vs insects): "
      f"{phyla_age - clade(phyla, ['Chordata', 'Arthropoda']).depth:.0f} Mya")
print(f"animals vs fungi:  "
      f"{euk_age - clade(euk, ['Mammalia', 'Agaricomycetes']).depth:.0f} Mya")
print(f"animals vs choanoflagellates: "
      f"{euk_age - clade(euk, ['Mammalia', 'Choanoflagellata']).depth:.0f} Mya")
print(f"animals vs plants: {euk_age:.0f} Mya")
```

The animals-versus-plants line needs no `clade()` call: that split is the
deepest one in this file, so the MRCA is the root itself and the
divergence is just the root's age. And note it is older than the
animal-fungus split (1,275 Mya): fungi are our closer cousins.


Single-celled
flagellates that strain bacteria out of water, the **choanoflagellates**,
split from us ~894 Mya; they are the closest living relatives of all
animals.

## Final task · Design your own tree of life

The final task has two stages. First compare the same evolutionary event
across two TimeTree files. Then use one of the eukaryote files to design and
save your own tree-of-life visualisation.

### 1 · Compare the two trees

The amniote family tree put the amniote root at **319 Myr**.
The eukaryote class tree is a completely different file, built from a
different set of studies at a different taxonomic rank, but it contains
`Mammalia` and `Aves` as tips. Write a `divergence(root, a, b)` helper
and use it to date the mammal–bird split in *this* tree, then compare.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_split
import js
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pyodide.http import open_url

DATA_URL = js.location.href.split("site_libs/")[0] + "data/"

class Node:
    def __init__(self, name="", length=0.0):
        self.name = name
        self.length = length
        self.children = []
        self.parent = None
    def is_leaf(self):
        return not self.children
    def leaves(self):
        return [self] if self.is_leaf() else [l for c in self.children for l in c.leaves()]
    def walk(self):
        yield self
        for c in self.children:
            yield from c.walk()

def parse_newick(text):
    s = text.strip().rstrip(";")
    pos = 0
    def read_label():
        nonlocal pos
        if pos < len(s) and s[pos] == "'":
            end = s.index("'", pos + 1)
            label, pos = s[pos + 1:end], end + 1
        else:
            start = pos
            while pos < len(s) and s[pos] not in ",():;":
                pos += 1
            label = s[start:pos]
        return label.strip()
    def read_length():
        nonlocal pos
        if pos < len(s) and s[pos] == ":":
            pos += 1
            start = pos
            while pos < len(s) and s[pos] not in ",();":
                pos += 1
            return float(s[start:pos])
        return 0.0
    def read_node():
        nonlocal pos
        node = Node()
        if s[pos] == "(":
            pos += 1
            while True:
                child = read_node()
                child.parent = node
                node.children.append(child)
                if s[pos] != ",":
                    break
                pos += 1
            pos += 1
        node.name = read_label()
        node.length = read_length()
        return node
    return read_node()

def set_depths(root):
    for node in root.walk():
        node.depth = (node.parent.depth if node.parent else 0.0) + node.length

def clade(root, names):
    want = set(names)
    best = None
    for node in root.walk():
        have = {l.name for l in node.leaves()}
        if want <= have and (best is None or len(have) < len(best[0])):
            best = (have, node)
    return best[1] if best else None

euk = parse_newick(open_url(DATA_URL + "eukaryotes_class.nwk").read())
set_depths(euk)
```

**Save your final tree-of-life visualisation.** After the figure is complete,
run this cell to download a 300 dpi PNG from the browser:

```{pyodide}
import base64
from io import BytesIO

def download_figure(fig, filename="eukaryote-tree-of-life.png"):
    buffer = BytesIO()
    fig.savefig(buffer, format="png", dpi=300,
                bbox_inches="tight", facecolor="white")
    encoded = base64.b64encode(buffer.getvalue()).decode("ascii")
    link = js.document.createElement("a")
    link.href = "data:image/png;base64," + encoded
    link.download = filename
    js.document.body.appendChild(link)
    link.click()
    link.remove()

download_figure(fig)
```

## Conclusion

When reading or constructing a phylogeny visualisation:

- **Only the nodes and branch lengths carry information.** The vertical
  order of tips is arbitrary: every internal node can be flipped.
  Humans are not "at the
  end" of the tree, because every living thing is exactly the same distance from
  the root.
- **The level of aggregation is part of the claim**. At phylum level no lineage dies in the great extinctions.
- **Every internal node is an inference**. Some are genuinely
  contested: e.g. whether sponges or comb jellies split from the rest of the
  animals first.

## Bonus

Read Long et al. (2025), [*Earliest amniote tracks recalibrate the timeline
of tetrapod evolution*](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12119326/).
Dates on a phylogenetic tree are estimates: fossils help to date its branches,
and new fossil evidence can revise those dates. The tracks described in this
paper push the likely origin of crown-group amniotes back by at least 35–40
million years.

## Sources

- Kumar et al. (2022) *TimeTree 5: an expanded resource for species
  divergence times*, Molecular Biology and Evolution 39:msac174;
  [timetree.org](https://timetree.org). Trees downloaded via "Build a
  Timetree" (group: Amniota at family rank; Eukaryota at class and phylum
  rank), Newick format, branch lengths in Myr; values unmodified.
- Names with suffixes (`Cebidae-1`, `Cebidae-2`) are TimeTree's way of
  serving groups that its consensus does not recover as single clades:
  the name is split, the tree is left honest.
- Tobias et al. (2022) AVONET and Myhrvold et al. (2015): the Part A
  datasets this page's amniotes connect back to.
